utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you call -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to mention a couple of brief matters.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought we were hearing from Dr. Greve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it "Dr." or "Judge" or "Miss".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, yes. Mr. Tieger will take over in a short moment. There are a couple of matters I wanted to mention, if I may? Firstly, your Honours, we would just like to notify a change in the order of witnesses. I mentioned it to the Defence, but the witness Medunjanin, Anes Medunjanin -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What number is that on your witness list?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Currently No. 11, your Honour. This witness is not available. We have not been able to make contact with the witness at the moment; we expect to be able to do so but we have not been able to at the moment. So we are seeking to replace that witness spot No. 11 by the witness Jerko Doko. He is currently No. 16.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see, he is No. 16 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness Mirsad Mujadzic, currently No. 14, we seek to put him following the witness Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Semenovic, your Honour, and that witness is No. 10.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So 14 will go before 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After 10.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: After 10, OK. So, we have just saved three to five hours! I am sorry, I am just joking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the scheme of things, it is not tremendously important. OK. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, there is. Your Honours, we received a notice that next week this Chamber is, apparently, going to be used for a matter on Tuesday morning, and there is another matter on Wednesday morning and so we will not be sitting until Wednesday afternoon. We have also heard there is to be, not a deferral hearing, a Rule 61 hearing, set for sometime in June/July which, apparently, may take as long as 10 days We are becoming somewhat concerned, your Honours, that with respect to next week, we have witnesses here who are arriving today we cannot stop who were planning to give evidence early next week who will probably be pushed right back to the end of next week or maybe into the next week because of these changes. I am just wondering, your Honours, is there any possibility that we could sit somewhere else or that other matters could be placed somewhere else in the building? I just raise it because it will seriously lengthen the trial if these interruptions are to come as regularly as they have been up until now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have - at the close of testimony today, I will talk to you about our schedule next week, but since you have raised it, yes, you are right, there is a deferral hearing set for Tuesday 28th in the morning. With respect to using another location, believe me, Mr. Niemann, I have lost sleep over the schedule, not the length of time that the Prosecutor is taking, but the number of intrusions that I know that we will have on this trial. There is a possibility of using the room that we used for pretrial, but there are logistical problems, equipment problems, money problems; believe me, I am very sympathetic to the desire of everyone to proceed as quickly as possible and we are doing the best that we can, but we just have other matters, this Chamber has other matters, it has to hear. As far as the other Trial Chamber, I will not speak for the other Trial Chamber, but perhaps they do have matters that are coming up as well. We have one courtroom and it took us a while to get this courtroom, but at least we have it and that is all that we have at the moment. We will do the best that we can. You are perfectly correct in raising that concern because I have asked you to present your case more efficiently and more expeditiously, and then there are all these intrusions into the schedule that have nothing to do with the Prosecution. You are right and correct. We will do the best that we can. I will inform you at the close of the testimony today regarding our schedule for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, will you call Dr. Greve? DR. GREVE recalled Examined by MR. TIEGER, continued

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, you may be seated, please. You are still under oath; you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, before the adjournment yesterday, we were speaking about the dissemination of propaganda related to Serbian nationalism and Serbian imperilment. In that connection, I wonder if I might ask Exhibit 85 to be brought to the witness's attention very quickly? (Handed). Can we have that document focused on the top of the page, please? Dr. Greve, do you see the date indicated on the article entitled the "The Glory of all Serbian Glories"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do and I forget yesterday to mention that this has been wrongly translated as 1st June; it should actually be 1st July. I recognise this because it is the celebration of St. Vitus Day. That is, I do not read Serbo Croatian myself, so I am unable to read the original text, but St. Vitus Day is celebrated on 28th June, so it has to be 1st July. It was checked with the translators, it is 1st July, so that is a mistake, unfortunately, in the document presented. I also have to apologise. I made a bad guess yesterday when I equated Prince Lazar with St. Vitus. The correct version (and I checked this this morning) is that Prince Lazar, the prince, the Serbian prince who is so well respected and celebrated in Serbian history, died on 15th June, that is, on the day of St. Vitus. That is why they celebrate him and St. Vitus at the same day. The reason also why I wanted, of course, to correct my own bad guess of yesterday -- I did say it was a guess and I am happy I did say that at least -- is also because it brings attention to a fact that confused me during my study of Prijedor area, and that is the distinction between the Julian and the Gregorian calendar. As you will know, we all use (or most of the world today uses) the Gregorian calendar. It was initially the Julian calendar which was adopted by Emperor Julius Caesar before Christ, adopted by the Christian world 325 AD and revised by Pope Grego, I think it was XIII, in 1582, because there was not full correspondence between the solar year and the year of the calendar. So although we have leap years to compensate, we had three leap years too much in 400 years. So in 1582, 10 days were crossed out of the calendar; some call it the Gregorian calendar; some call it the revised Julian calendar. But the significance of this is that th orthodox church with reference to celebration of religious feast use reference to the old and not revised Julian calendar. That is, sometimes I came across witnesses who gave me a date, for instance, of Petrovdan which varied with a fortnight from what others said and I was, it made me insecure, and I wondered if they were that mistaken when they were referring to these holidays. But the truth is that in the year 1992, which is our focus, there is a fortnight between the Julian calendar and our Gregorian calendar. That is, 1st January 1992 in the Julian calendar comes on 14th January 1992 in the Gregorian calendar. So there is a difference and, if I may say so, if it comes to reference to feasts, it may be useful to ask according to which calendar if a date is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, I would like to move now to 1990: Following the breakdown of the communist system in Yugoslavia, were democratic elections held in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In opstina of Prijedor, which were the main political parties involved in that election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the SDA, the party of Democrat Action; it was the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party; it was the HDZ which was the Croatian Democratic Union, and there were some leftist parties, the Reformists, the Liberals, etc., and Ante Markovic actually had his founding ceremony for the Reformist party held in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who were among the leaders in Prijedor in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several leaders in the SDA. Actually, their names have been referred to when it comes to sources mainly by witnesses, but some of them are also reported in the later newspaper articles; among them Muhamed Cehajic who became the Lord Mayor; Mirsad Mujadzic who was from the Ljubija area; Hilmija Hopovac who was from that same area. I do also know a number of names from the Kozarac area, but only from witness statements, and I have not had these names confirmed from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who were among the leaders of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among the leaders of the SDS were Srdo Srdic; it was Simo Miskovic; it was Milan Stakic; it was Miko Kovacevic; it was Simo Drljaca and Slobodan Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those are names we will be hearing about further in the testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these are all names that is being mentioned in all the public reports as well, so their names, I have heard them both from witnesses and from the local media; many of them have given interviews, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the outcome of the elections in Prijedor in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outcome of the election, let me immediately mention, there is a local Assembly in Prijedor which has 90 seats. According to the votes, the seats were distributed with 28 seats for the SDS, the Serbian party, with 30 seats for the SDA, the Muslim party, and two seats for the HDZ, the Croat party, and 30 seats for other parties. That is a considerable amount of seats were distributed to parties that did not link so much to any particular group and, of course, this was the first ever free election in a multi-party system. So it was a very young democracy that went to throw their ballot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did this plurality victory by the SDA mean they were in a position to fill all appointed political positions with its members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For (1) democracy means to distribute this according to the vote. So it was, of course, reflected the composition of the Assembly as other political positions were reflecting the position between the parties; but also it is my understanding that Tito's Yugoslavia was built on very elaborate keys for the division of positions according to ethnic groups, so that all of them would be represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So after the election, the appointed positions to be filled were to be distributed among the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were all the positions immediately filled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not all of them, that is to say, there were no positions that were left vacant, but they were not immediate changes in all of them, according to the outcome of the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were some of the positions filled within a reasonable amount of time after the election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. That is, essentially, the political position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As time went on, were the remaining positions agreed upon? Was there a consensus reached on which party member should occupy which appointed position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not without some bickering, but eventually they were, yes, distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the bickering that took place in the Assembly decrease, remain the same or increase over time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been quite difficult immediately and it has to be kept in mind that it is an enormous step for any one society to move from a totalitarian communist regime to become a democracy. One cannot just click fingers and it is done with that; it is a process it has to do with learning. I think it was difficult from the very start, but as ethnic hatred or propaganda started it became even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As time went on, did the Serbs in Prijedor begin to establish their own separate political structure outside of the existing democratic institutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and that was also in the light of what happened outside the opstina as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was a separate Assembly or any other institution established by the Serbs in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually there was a separate Assembly set up. Initially, people did not know much about it. Later, we have received documents that verify this. But what witnesses told us, or told me, reported, was that there were some kind of meetings, they considered it to be peculiar meetings, among the Serb politicians. They were not so sure if this was just meetings so that they would prepare themselves before they came into the Assembly or if it was some kind of a separate structure, but they were wondering. Essentially, they were sort of not too keen on knowing what this exactly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the establishment of this separate Serbian Assembly an independent act by local Serbian political authorities or was it done at someone else's direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was happening in co-operation between the local Serbs and the central SDS, Serbian party, administration and the separate Serbian structures that at this time were being developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have these documents marked, please, for identification as Exhibit 91? (Handed) (To the witness): Dr. Greve, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is again an article from Kozarski Vjesnik, this time dated 28th April 1994. The caption is how Dr. Milomir Stakic, first Chairman of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, saw the events of 30th April and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Prosecution 91?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 91 will be admitted. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): Dr. Greve, let me direct your attention to that portion of the article you just indicated at the top of page 1. At the top of the page, does it indicate that Dr. Milomir Stakic was the first Chairman of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, the institution to which you were just referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I hasten to add he was the Vice, he was the Deputy Mayor in the official structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to paragraph (3), you see the sentence in the approximate middle of the paragraph that begins, "On the direction"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Does that article indicate at whose direction the separate Serbian Assembly of Prijedor was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it indicates that this was established at the direction of the SDS, Srpska Demokrastka Stranka, which is the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was that the local SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, this is the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The central office of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the way I would look at it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Where is the central office then of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina -- at the time that would be in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour, that is fine. (To the witness): In addition to the establishment of a separate Municipal Assembly outside the democratic government, was any other separate institution created by Serb officials in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, particularly, in particular, there was the setup of a separate police, and the main source of the information about the separate police is again the interview that was given about a year after by head of the Serbian police, Simo Drljaca. When he was promoted to become the vice Minister of Interior, he was explaining how he had been working. He used the word or it is translated as "illegally", how he was setting up an illegal entity of Serbian police working on this for months or half a year approximately prior to 30th April 1992. That was a complete structure for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, may I have these documents marked for identification as Exhibit 92? (To the witness): Dr. Greve, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the article from Kozarski Vjesnik dated 9th April 1994 (sic) which is an interview with Simo Drljaca, then Deputy Minister of Interior, of the Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Looking at, you said April 9th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, it is 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That contains an interview with Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 92 will be admitted. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): Dr. Greve, can I direct your attention then to the top of the first page of that article? On April 9th, 1993, what was Simo Drljaca's position within the declared Serb Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was designated Deputy Minister of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In 1992 what was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, from 30th April onwards, he was head of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the second line of this article -- let me direct your attention first to the first line. Does the interview with Simo Drljaca indicate who selected him to set up these illegal police stations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is indicated that it was done by the Serb Democratic Party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Does the article indicate when that work began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: How long before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six months before the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: As a result of Simo Drljaca's efforts to establish an illegal police force, how many stations were created manned by how many officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A force of 1,775 well-armed men in 13 police stations, is his figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was the establishment of this illegal Police Force by Serb officials done in co-operation with any other group in Prijedor other than the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the army, and that was at the time the JNA, the army of the Yugoslavian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this document marked as exhibit 93 for identification, please? (Handed). (To the witness): Dr. Greve, what is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is another newspaper article from Kozarski Vjesnik dated 19th November 1993. It is headlined "21 November, the day of Security Services of Republica Srpska".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 93 will be admitted. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): Dr. Greve, may I direct your attention then to the third paragraph of that article? Does the article also confirm the establishment of illegal Serbian police stations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It refers to 30 illegal Serbian police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Does the article also indicate who participated in the establishment of the illegal police stations and the takeover of power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it states explicitly that all the preparations had been carried out in an exemplary co-operation with the Serbian army, and this was still the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Look at the top of the page, the event which prompted this article was what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a celebration, actually it celebrates, and again it links the celebration of the police to the celebration of the day of the Arch Angel Mihajlo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were the police, the Serbian police, in Prijedor closely linked to Serbian officials outside the opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, and again our best source is head of police, Simo Drljaca, head of police at 30th April 1992, because he is confirming that he worked closely with the central authorities in Banja Luka, and that they again took the orders straight from what is called Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have the previous exhibit, Exhibit 92, presented to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be the Minister of Interior of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I hasten, or I should immediately add that one may be slightly confused with the wording "Republic" in this context. We will, I think, explain it in detail a little later, but the Republika Srpska was never declared as an independent state; it was always said that it was one, it was one federal unit within the great Serbian state with Serbia proper and with these four areas that had been taken under Serb control in Croatia. So it is not to be confused with an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say that it was said that it was a unit of Serbia, it was said by persons in the Republic of Srpska that it was a unit of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was proclaimed, when they proclaimed Republika Srpska, or actually they started with proclaiming, and we will have the documentation coming, they started with proclaiming Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they were pointing out at that point that they did not want to become a state, but they declared to be in statehood with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have a feeling that I am getting ahead of this story, and so I will retreat. The question that I had though really related to not what was the intention of the Republic of Srpske vis-a-vis the relationship with Serbia, but the reaction of Serbia to that proclamation, not an official proclamation but at least the position taken by the Republik of Srpska, but we will get to that later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I may, if it can of any assistance -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know whether Mr. Tieger would enjoy that, interrupting his direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no objection whatsoever in disrupting .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will hear it in tandem. We will hear it at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I may give you, your Honour, one indication, and that is when this separate structure is being set up, it is with full co-operation of the JNA, that is, the army of the country with which they want to belong in statehood. Of course, there is still a linkage between the Serb Republic and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but even after the breach when Bosnia-Herzegovina becomes independent or declares independence in early April 1992 and up to the Serbs are taking power in Prijedor, there are at least 24 days, and in this period the JNA exists and it fully cooperates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: At this time was the Belgrade government calling itself Serbia, Serbian, or did it still call itself Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the references we just seen to Serbian co-operation or the Serbian army really is a misnomer, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this, of course, is a newspaper article when they are communicating with the local people, and then it is perhaps considered convenient to use the then new names. That is perhaps the way I have tended to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you know where you are?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Just to clarify the chronology a bit, Simo Drljaca was the man designated by the SDS in Prijedor to establish the illegal police stations in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then after the military takeover of Prijedor he became the Chief of Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was thereafter that he was appointed, promoted to the position of Deputy Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What is the relationship between the Ministry of the Interior and the police department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may say a few general words about this? It has to be kept in mind that what we are seeing is an old totalitarian regime that is changing to become more democratic. In the old communist setting, one of the key ministries were the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Interior would be the one in charge of both the secret police, state police and public security police issues. The Ministry of Justice would, in comparison, be a tiny and not so important entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had asked you about the connection between the police in Prijedor and Serbian entities outside the opstina. Can I ask you to look at the bottom of page 2 of Exhibit 92? Looking at that document, the interview with Simo Drljaca, then the Deputy Minister of the Interior, does he indicate the relationship between the police in Prijedor and entities outside ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that is the Serbian police, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is actually at this time he is answering to some criticism, and he is saying that if something, quoting the last sentence in the paragraph, "If something was not done correctly, then I should be replaced and not they because they executed my orders and those from the chief of the central police headquarters in Banja Luka and the Minister of the Interior".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the separate Serbian Assembly of Prijedor was established at the direction of the central office of the SDS. I would like to discuss the links between that separate Assembly in Prijedor and the separate Serbian structures outside of Prijedor. In that connection, may I have this marked as Exhibit 94 for identification? (Handed) What is that document, Dr. Greve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a decision dated 17th January 1992. It states that it is a decision to unite with the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina and article (1) states that -----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, before you proceed with the document, I would like to tender that for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 94?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 94 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can the document be placed on the screen, please? (To the witness): Dr. Greve, you indicated that this was a decision reached on January 17th 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again that decision was -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a decision to unite with the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is a decision by which institution to unite with the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian People's Assembly in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was signed by the individual you referred to earlier, Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As Chairman of the Serbian People's Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the time he was also the Vice President of the democratically elected Assembly in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, what was the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina that is referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time it was a region similar to the regions previously proclaimed in Croatia as SAOs, Serbian autonomous -- Srpska Autonomna Oblast, that is, Serbian autonomous districts. Krajina, I should say, is an area to be divided by the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, so you have one region of Krajina in Croatia and another region of Krajina in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For what reason they already existed a sole, an autonomous region of Krajina. That is why one is using now a different name for the autonomous region on the Bosnian side of Krajina; it is called a region and not an "oblast".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the autonomous region part of the democratically elected government within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was set up and step by step moved further away to be completely autonomous from the government in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the first step in the creation of this separate autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may, perhaps, say that before any steps were taken, there were no such thing as total regional structures. There were two main Chambers of Commerce in north western Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there were some financial co-operation and there were some association of municipalities to do co-ordinated planning and trade, which was obviously very good and very welcome. But then at one point, that is, late April 1991, late April 1991, there was a change in this structure, and the autonomous region of Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, becomes an entity which also takes upon it to have some military independence. That is firmly objected to by the government in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is not yet -- the Republic is not yet independent, but still the legal authorities all seated in Sarajevo and they object to this creation. Only in September 1991, there is a formal declaration of independence for the ARK, Autonomous Region Krajina, which is the entity located within Bosnia-Herzegovina in contra-distinction to the South Krajina on the other side of the border, that is, inside Croatia. So it is two entities with the name "Krajina" because the area is not so naturally divided in a sense, the name is found in both areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In April 1991 when an association of municipalities in the Krajina region took on some military aspects rather than purely economic co-operative aspects, did it call itself the autonomous region at that time or did it continue to call itself an association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was moving towards autonomy already at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it known as the autonomous region of Krajina or was it known as the association of municipalities in April when it took on these military aspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am perhaps not exactly sure of that, because I think at this time I think it called itself autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina, but it left out the name "Bosanska" later -- but I may be mistaken on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me have, if I may, this document marked as Exhibit 95 for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you, I hope this is idle curiosity but we have come across "Bosanska" in a number of place names, has it got a meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it means "Bosnian".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that is the reason, and that adds to some confusion, or it did on my part: At a later stage one of the things that the separate Serbian structure is eager to do is to cross out the reference to anything that is Bosnian. So when it is called Bosanska Krajina, it becomes "Krajina"; if a city is named Bosanska Novi, Bosanski Gradica, it changes the name, leaves out "Bosnian". MR. TIEGER (To the witness): Dr. Greve, can I ask you to look at Exhibit 95 marked for identification? What is that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is again a translation of a newspaper article which appeared in the newspaper, Oslobodenje, which is printed in Sarajevo. It is dated 24th May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 95 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If that could be placed on the screen, please? (To the witness): Does this document indicate the reaction to the establishment of a separate association in the Krajina region at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is noting that the SDA, the party of Democratic Action, that is, the one associated with the Muslims in Banja Luka, are strongly opposed to the idea of creating what they call a state within a state.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, I have a question, I guess, a confusion, about how this operated from a practical point of view. You had a General Assembly in Prijedor. The SDA received not the majority but received the largest number of votes of 30 seats, I guess, out of 90. Then you say there were 30 others. I do not know how these others aligned with the SDA. But when the SDS was developing these relationships with other areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example, the relationship with Krajina, what was the reaction of the leaders in the General Assembly? Did the SDS continue to participate in the Assembly in Prijedor and at the same time try to create an autonomous state of Bosnian Serbs in Prijedor and align with other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were predominantly Serb? What was the reaction within the General Assembly? It would seem to me that the SDA and other parties would respond within the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, most of those key people from other parties than the SDS -- from other parties than the Serbian parties and outside the Serbian group are dead, meaning that we have not been able to question them about this particular issue, but the information we had which is second-hand, I admit, is that people did not fully understand this. It was in a sense so much happening in Eastern Europe in general, confusion; transition; communism breaking down; it was combined with financial crisis; democracy was being established; republics were considering to leave the Federation; people were confused. They were not used to be tuned into political thinking like people in a democracy, that is, it always used to be decided by the party what was to be the line of the country. So many people, it seems to me from secondary sources, I admit, did not really feel that they knew enough about the situation to be really alerted in time. They were taken by surprise. They saw that certain things were happening, but to a degree their reaction was more that this was peculiar than that this was dangerous. But when it came to the independent or autonomous regions, as we will come to Prijedor through its Assembly, the elected Assembly refused to join this entity. But all parties remained within the elected Assembly, but it became more and more difficult to operate in that Assembly as previously indicated. If I also may answer your first question, which was, what about the 30 votes which were distributed between different other parties? As indicated, Reformists and the Liberal Party which were some, what shall I say, reawakened communist parties -- maybe that is not the right way to describe them -- it is leftist parties, and people would join them from different groups, and the mere fact that one-third of the population did not vote along the lines of these three main parties, that is, being associated with specific ethnic groups, indicates that, perhaps, people did not think that ethnic groups had anything really to do in politics at this time. Many Serbs, and they will blame this afterwards both in newspaper articles and according to also Serb people with whom we have been speaking, had voted for other parties than the SDS, the Serbian Democrat Party. But eventually it became no more acceptable for a Serb not to be of true Serbian nationalist thinking, that was also to join the party. There are actually decisions made in the independent region of Krajina to the effect that to be a real Serb and have any leading position or be entrusted, one should be a party member and know that guidance of the Serb people was firmly taken care of by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Referring to this association or entity that was established in April of '91, was that constitutionally challenged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this document marked as Exhibit 96 for identification, please? (Document handed). (To the witness): What is that document, Dr. Greve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a ruling which is published in the official gazette of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is still within the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May that be placed on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 96 will be admitted. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): Dr. Greve, looking at the top of the page, that is a decision by which institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the session held on 1st November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The ruling concerns which institution as indicated in that first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It concerns the Association of Bosanska Krajina municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And focuses on the agreement to join the association of Bosanska Krajina municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The ruling by the constitutional court is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is that this decision will be null and void.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That ruling was on November 1st 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By that time, had the Association of Bosanska Krajina municipalities become the autonomous region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, I would like to ask you which municipalities in the area joined the autonomous region, and it might be helpful if I had Exhibit 73 displayed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is this the entire decision while we are locating 73?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, not what is depicted on the screen, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was just wondering whether there is any reasoning or rationale. All I see is a declaration it is null and void.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is contained in the documents which has been tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are offering the entire decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the so-called justification that is added on the following pages. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): Dr. Greve, does this map assist you in indicating the municipalities which joined the autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am just waiting to get on the screen the exact -- yes. What we can see is, if we start to the west of Prijedor, we see Bosanski Novi which joined; to the north of Prijedor we see Bosanski Djubica which joined; we see Bosanski Gradiska which joined; and I am afraid I cannot read on my screen -- oh, I can -- it is Srbac which joined; it is Prnjavor which joined; it is Laktasi which joined; Banja Luka joining; Celinac joining, and I skip Kotor Varos which did not join, Skender Vakuf joining; Mrkonjic Grad joining; Sipovo, and then I move further south, I mention Kljuc which joined; Sipovo joined; Kupres joined; Glamoc joined; Bosanski Grahovo, Titov Drvar joined and Bosanski Petrovac joined. In what is called Bosanski Kupres the river Una comes done along this border and flows through Bosanski Kupres. So there was a part of Bosanski Kupres which was referred to as Kupres, now "Una", the part which is to the east of the River Una, which was Serb controlled, and that part also associated itself. But important to point out in this context is, perhaps, that Prijedor became isolated with three other or two other provinces in the area. Sanski Most did not join. Prijedor did not join, that is, the legally elected Assembly of Prijedor did not join, and Kotor Varos did not join.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What eventually happened to Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all ethnically cleansed, so-called, by violent means and force and they then joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Serbian authorities also form a separate political entity on the republic level as well as the Municipal and regional level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was that entity called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, it was the politicians that were participants in the legal parliament in Sarajevo, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They together with other representatives of the Serb people on 9th January 1992, 9th January 1992, declared a republic, but again a republic as being a federal unit wanting to be in statehood with what I, for reasons of convenience, call Serbia proper and the autonomous Serb areas in Croatia, and they formed what was called at the time the Republic of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- a name which was changed on 28th February to be the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a name which was changed again on 12th August 1992 to be Republika Srpska. There was no other main changes than this change in name, so the entity is the same whatever the name it is referred to. It only has a difference in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the separate Serbian Assembly in November or in October call for the holding of a plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did, 21st October it decided to ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this document marked as Exhibit 97 for identification? (Document handed). (To the witness): Dr. Greve, what is Exhibit 97 for identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a ballot paper which was used in the plebiscite held in October, sorry, in November 1991, and in which the Serbian people in, particular were, asked in what kind of statehood relationship they would want to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We tender 97 for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 97 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May that be put on the screen, please? (To the witness): Dr. Greve, what is the general issue presented by this plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should perhaps indicate immediately that this ballot paper is actually -- in one paper we have two different ballot papers, and what is being shown at the screen at the moment is the ballot paper which is given to the people of Serb ethnic background, those who declare themselves as Serbs. They are asked to vote and indicate whether they are in favour of a decision reached by the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina on 21st October 1991, whereby the Serbian people shall remain in the common state of Yugoslavia which would include Serbia, Montenegro, SAO Krajina, SAO Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem along with all others willing to remain in such a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How was the ballot framed for non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is shown and indicated on this same paper. It was formulated differently for the non-Serbs. They are asked if they are in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining a republic with equal status in a common state of Yugoslavia with all the other republics which also declared themselves willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Aside from the reference to the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the ballot presented to Serbs, is there any mention of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the common state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I ask you to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. In the ballot presented to non-Serbs where it indicates whether or not the Serbian people shall remain in a common state of Yugoslavia, and list the members of that common state, is Bosnia-Herzegovina indicated anywhere? I am sorry, I misspoke. This is the ballot presented to Serbs, excuse me. Does the -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, excuse me, I was a bit slow. I am sorry. No, in the ballot paper presented to the Serbs there is no indication of the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as such. Here we are only -- they are only referring to these autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did most Serbs vote in the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a few non-Serbs voting, but I have not seen any figures for how many participated. It is my understanding it was relatively few.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the plebiscite regarded as an important event by Serbian officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later it is actually -- whether or not one had participated in this plebiscite is considered significant as to have demonstrated one's true understanding of what it means to be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was its importance in part affirmed by the subsequent declaration of a wholly separate Serbian entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask that Exhibit 50 be shown to the witness? (Document handed).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, maybe this is very naive on my part, but how did the election for the plebiscite take place or how did the voting take place? One ballot was given to Serbs; would people line up and show some proof that they were Serb and they would get the ballot for Serbs, and then there would be another line of people who would demonstrate that they were non-Serbs, and they would get the other ballot? Is that the way it operated and, if so, what about the people who were mixed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding for (1) that the word, it was spread by word of mouth. This I have from witnesses and information gathered in general. I have not been able to see any newspaper article listing this completely, but I understand that Serbs were approached informally and told that it was appreciated that they would go and vote. Everyone was asked to vote. According to non-Serbs who came to vote, it was a question whether they had to be registered on this list or that list. It is like going to vote in our countries; we will be marked off on whether we come to vote or not. There would be separate lists for Serbs. If at this time people also, which there is some indication to, could sort of declare themselves as Serbs, if they came from a mixed background and had not considered themselves Serbs before, possibly they could do that. I am not completely sure on it. But those who said, "I am a non-Serb" were at least be given the ballot paper for non-Serbs. That is my understanding. I apologise it is superficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could follow up on the court's question and recall the previous exhibit, Exhibit 97, before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The two ballots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Linked to the two ballots, there is also an instruction as to how to proceed and it is for the Serb Democratic Party to organise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could page 2 of that document be displayed on the elmo? (To the witness): Accompanying the article in which the ballot or copies of the two ballots are shown, are there also instructions, specific instructions, for how the voting should take place and who should organise it? Dr. Greve, I am sorry, I am just identifying that portion of document. Does it indicate that organs were established for the conduct of the plebiscite and instructions on how to undertake that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning to the last page of that document, are there instructions on how the ballots are to be presented to individuals who appeared to vote in the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. There is, however, there is one interesting point in this, if I may say so. It is not particularly clear whether an identity card at this moment would already indicate national background or ethnic group, but possibly this could be read out of the ID card and the numbers already, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It indicates that the ballots would have separate colours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yellow for the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask a question at this stage? Bearing in mind the long years of communism in Yugoslavia, if one was completely irreligious, how would anyone know that one was Serb or Croat or Muslim? Would it just be by common repute, the language will be the same, the true ethnicity would be the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This, your Honour, is a very good question which a number of people have told me they asked themselves because they simply said, "I have lost track; I have two grandparents from this group and one from each of the others. I never practised religion. Our language is the same. We cannot be distinguished by features or anything". It was not common in the period of the communist regime to think in ethnic terms. One was a Yugoslav. So time and again people would come forward and say, "I really do not know. I am me, but I do not really find myself as belonging to this group as opposed to that group". But some people would live, and this was particularly, perhaps, in remote rural areas where there was more homogenous structure and people had lived and married within a tiny little circle for a long time, but particularly in the cities, there seems to be a lot of people who found themselves to be of such a mixed descent that it was a matter of choice to present yourself as this or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning back to page 3 of that document, does it indicate that the Commissions were to be established for the conducting of the plebiscite including a main Commission, a District Commission and then at the more local level election board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These were the instructions on how to conduct the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you have, aside from word of mouth, not seen articles on the manner in which it was actually conducted when it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can now return to Exhibit 50? Dr. Greve, I had asked you about the importance attached to the conducting of a plebiscite by Serbian officials, and whether or not the establishment of a separate Serbian entity affirmed that importance. In that connection I would like you to look at Exhibit 50 and ask that it be placed on the elmo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of that document does it indicate the basis on which the declaration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- is made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It refers to the plebiscite held on 19th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And indicates that it has done so on the basis of the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does and the Serbian people's decision in that plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, I appreciate that the discussion of these entities in a kind of chronological order maybe a bit confusing, so if I can have this marked for identification as Exhibit 98? What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a tiny organogramme which I made simply to visualise the different levels in the different structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 98 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May that be placed on the screen, please? (To the witness): What does the left side of the document indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The left side of the document indicates the legal structure in the time of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the different levels, administrative levels, the Republic, the Federal Republic level, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the regional level, which at that time was not that significant -- it was the two main Chambers of Commerce -- and the opstina level -- here indicated by opstina Prijedor -- and what I referred to yesterday as the Mjesna Zajednica meaning the local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What does the right side of the document describe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right side is made to indicate the separate structure which is being set up in 1991, 1992. On 27th April 1992, it is recalled from Dr. Gow's explanation that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was declared which is a legal entity. Then there are these new entities, and I have placed them sort of from the federal level and down to the commune level; the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was declared on 9th January 1992, changing its name, 28th February 1992, to become the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, changing again its name on 12th August 1992 to become Republika Srpska, and having declared itself in statehood with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This again operated with the autonomous regions. There were several of them. I have indicated the autonomous region of Krajina, which carries the acronym ARK, because that is the regional unit which is just about opstina Prijedor. When the Serbs took power in Prijedor, they declared it to be Srpska opstina Prijedor, meaning the Serbian opstina Prijedor, and still the local communes, which then became Serbian communes, remained Mjesna Zajednica. It is only to indicate the different levels as I myself find it easier to relate something sometimes to what is illustrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I note that on the left side, which indicates the democratically elected structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the region is marked but there is no box. In the official government, was there any regional structure analogous to the autonomous region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not. It was only these two Chambers of Commerce which had a very different background and level of functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am about to move on to a separate topic, your Honour, unless the court has questions?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I did have a question regarding 98, is it? Dr. Greve, on the right-hand side of the diagram, you have the boxes in dotted lines, the four boxes, below the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Why are they in dotted lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have put them in dotted lines because it is disputed if this is legal structures or not. They are objected to as being legally and lawfully established structures, but they are definitely de facto existing structures. I only did this to visualise something, but not to minimise the debate on that important issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is helpful to visualise it. But I also note that you do not have any arrows. When I think of an organisational chart, I think of something being at the top, and then there being arrows to show who reports to whom;is it the purpose of this chart to suggest or to establish that the Republic of Srpska reported to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As political science is not my field of expertise, I have purposely left out arrows so that I should not move beyond my own understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Greve, we have been discussing in general a period of time between the elections in August 1990 and the takeover in April 1992. I would like to take you to a point in the middle of that in 1991 when the war in Croatia erupted. Did that have an effect on ethnic relations in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did when it came to mobilization.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the national or ethnic groups respond differently as groups to the mobilization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did the Serbs respond to the mobilization to fight in the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In contradistinction to the non-Serbs, Serbs responded positively in principle. There were of course many among them as well who were hesitant to go to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the Muslim and Croat community response to the mobilization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general they did not respond, that is they would not be willing to fight in the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the SDA on a republic and opstina levels support the mobilization or opposed the mobilization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It opposed the mobilization.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did they take any steps, however, to physically obstruct the mobilization in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in principle, but they were quite eager to see at the time that there would be rather a reduction in armament and war efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did this disparate response by the ethnic groups create heightened tensions between those groups

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a certain extent I think it was most efficient in terms of being useful for the propaganda efforts, and the split being created by the Serbs being threatened and having many enemies among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there an increase in propaganda following the outbreak of the Croatian war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now did the different responses to the mobilization have an effect on arming within or on the level of arms within opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, with respect to those Serbs from Prijedor who responded to the mobilization what effect did it have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were armed and they were equipped and trained and sent to the theatre of war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When they returned to Prijedor, were they demobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not. There was a decision by the legal authorities in opstina Prijedor that they should be disarmed and demobilized, but that was not accepted and did not happen de facto.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Muslims who had previously been members of the reserve units become no longer part of those reserve units of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in part that happened, quite to some, a large extent I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now in addition to the arms received by Serbs who responded to the mobilization and who returned with those arms and were not demobilized, was there additional arming of persons within opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was considerable additional arming. The general population were not alarmed by the fact that soldiers going to war were being armed, but they started to be alarmed when they saw neighbours and Serbs in general being armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Serb citizens who were not part of the war in Croatia were also being armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, such as elderly women, young youngsters, clearly under age to go to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Serbian de facto officials in Prijedor later acknowledge this arming of citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this document marked as No. 99 for identification, please? (Document handed). Dr. Greve, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a newspaper article from Kozarski Vjesnik dated 9th July 1993 where it is excerpts from what was broadcast on Radio Prijedor in the programme Srdjan Mrdjan Maladan which was broadcast on 30th June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does it contain the presentation of a programme which included the participation of the Deputy Chairman of the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The commander of the 43rd Brigade Militia Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The head of the public security station in Prijedor at that time in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that No. 99 for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 99 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, can I draw your attention to page 3, please. Can the monitor be focused on the fifth paragraph. Dr. Greve, you see the fifth paragraph which is a Radanovic speaking according to the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who is Simo Radanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is the military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he an active leader during the time of, following the takeover and during the time of cleansings in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. According to himself he was the head of the so-called Gypsy Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he later become deputy Chairman of the Prijedor Municipality Assembly after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, according to himself and statements in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. Does he confirm whether or not there was arming of Serbs in opstina Prijedor before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, does he certify it in that first sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He says: "I hereby certify that, with agreement and co-operation of some countries Serbs at the time, we had indeed started the armament of Serbian people, but under condition that the abuse of weapons should be avoided."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is he speaking about the time prior to the military takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is that he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this document marked as Exhibit 100, please? (Document handed). What is this Exhibit, Dr. Greve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is again a translation of a newspaper article printed in Kozarski Vjesnik, 6th August 1993 with a headline: "Third Anniversary of the Serbian Democratic Party of Prijedor preventing a repetition of the Serbian massacre of 1941".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who is primarily quoted in this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several. Simo Miskovic, I think he is the one who is primarily quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We tender this document for admission, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 100?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 100 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May that be placed on the screen, please. Dr. Greve, you mentioned Simo Miskovic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was Chairman of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party District Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does the article at the top indicate the occasion which prompted the interview with Simo Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the third anniversary of the Serbian Democratic Party of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning to the last sentence in paragraph 3, does Simo Miskovic indicate whether or not Serbs were armed prior to the military takeover in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he acknowledged this, saying the SDS leadership saw what they were planning, referring to non-Serbs,and started to arm their own people in order to prevent the tragedy of 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I note in that same paragraph, Dr. Greve, in the second sentence it says that: "On August 2nd 1991 we in the district of Prijedor have formed the SDS." Is that an accurate date for the establishment of the SDS in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it cannot be as they participated in the election the previous year, but also, as this is printed in 1993, there could be a mistake in the original or in the translation, as this is called "the third anniversary" indicating, of course, that this party was established in Prijedor before participating in the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the process of arming Serbs by the SDS within opstina Prijedor accelerated as the time drew closer to the military takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection I ask you to look at Exhibit 91, if that can be presented to the witness. (Document handed). Dr. Greve, who participated in the arming of Serbs in the opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was again a joint effort between the party, the military and the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask that page 1 of Exhibit 91 be displayed on the screen? Can we focus on the fourth paragraph, please? Looking at that paragraph and the one on the next page, does it indicate the co-operation and assistance of the Commander of the army in Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It is actually referring in the last line to Colonel Arsic, Vladimir Arsic, who was the Commander in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we display the top of the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is stated that he was the Commander of "our garrison, a good soldier and a man with a lot of experience and we decided that we must speed up the process of arming ourselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All this was before April 30th 1992 when the takeover occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before the announced time of withdrawal for the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. If I may add something which I think is significant, which is that this process of armament, of arming the ordinary people, fed well into the line of propaganda, that is, people became even more fearful when they were told that they had to be armed to protect themselves, so as if there were enemies everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now in addition to the standing army, the JNA, the defence system of the former Yugoslavia also included Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which was in some practical effect a sort of republic army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were weapons of the TO under that system held by the local opstinas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that mean that in this case weapons were available to Muslims and Croats by virtue of the existence of the TO? A In principle, yes. In practice they had started to withdraw arms from the TO in 1991. This is one of the issues that I think Dr. Gow was looking into also with reference to the book of General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this document marked as Exhibit 101? (Document handed). Dr. Greve, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also a translation of an article in Kozarski Vjesnik dated 20th May 1994, headlined: "We know our goal".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It contains an interview with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Radmilo Zeljaja, Commander of the 33rd Prijedor Motorized Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We tender this document for admission, your Honour, 101.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 101 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can that be displayed on the screen, please, on page 1? Can we look to the second paragraph, please? Dr. Greve, looking at the middle of that paragraph, the sentence which begins "Our command", does Colonel Zeljaja indicate what happened to the weapons of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he does. He is saying that, "Our command, with the approval of the Corps," that is the one headquartered in Banja Luka, "managed to get together both the weapons and technical equipment from the Territorial Defence TO units of the municipalities, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Novi Grad and Bosanski Dubica, as well as Kninska Krajina region, and place them under our control in our depots."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So those TO weapons would at that point be under the physical control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding from the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of these weapons were later redistributed to the TOs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In general what amounts and what quality weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general it was just a small amount of the total number of weapons, and it was not good quality weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now in addition to having a separate Police Force and a separate Assembly, did Serbs authorities refer to a Serbian TO, a separate TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They started to refer to a Serbian TO prior to taking power on 30th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who was the head of that Serbian Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Slobodan Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this document marked as Exhibit 102 for identification, please? (Document handed). What is this document, Dr. Grieve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
